subject: Re: Combining aerial photography and MRDS

messages.author: 7a370588160d954e
messages.subject: Combining aerial photography and MRDS
parts:
Hi folks,

We conducted an aerial survey for narwhals using a double-observer distan=
ce sampling protocol. Concurrently, using two cameras angled obliquely, w=
e took aerial photos of the area directly below the plane and out to eith=
er side. Approximately a third of the area covered by the photographs was=
also visible to the observers.=20

The plan is to conduct MRDS analysis in Distance to calculate the abundan=
ce of the population. Unfortunately, two of our observers, one on either =
side, appear to have missed many observations or not measured declination=
angles. Specifically, they did not site many animals missed by the other=
two more-experienced observers. I consequently suspect that we will not =
have a sufficient correction of =E2=80=9Cperception bias=E2=80=9D (animal=
s visible but not observed). We know from previous surveys that our obser=
vers are missing animals at the trackline and would like to correct this =
negative bias. To be clear, we know that animals are being missed within =
the region visible to the observers at the bubble windows, not only direc=
tly below the plane.=20

I=E2=80=99m wondering if there is a way to use the aerial photographs to =
correct for missed animals. Unfortunately, we have approximately 40,000 p=
hotos and no time to view them all. Our sightings are quite patchy, with =
many transects having 0 sightings. I=E2=80=99m wondering if anyone has a =
suggestion for an effective way to sub-sample the photos to establish a c=
orrection factor for the visual observations. Specifically, could we focu=
s our efforts on transects with sightings? The narwhal density is likely =
low enough that randomly sub-sampling the photos may not lead to many sig=
htings.=20

Any advice would be greatly appreciated. Feel free to respond directly to=
me and I=E2=80=99ll collate the responses and post them back to the list=
.=20

Sincerely, Natalie.=20=20

messages.subject: Re: Combining aerial photography and MRDS
parts:
Hi folks,

Thanks for the replies (copied below). Regarding David and Len=E2=80=99s =
suggestion of setting up =E2=80=9Ctrials=E2=80=9D for the visual observer=
s using the photos and then doing a Trial-observer MRDS analysis, one pro=
blem I can foresee is that we had high densities in relatively open water=
, near sea ice, and very low densities in sea ice. Detection in open wate=
r is much easier than detection in sea ice. So, we definitely need to set=
up some trials in sea ice to check if the low densities are true low den=
sities or a lack of detection due to sea ice.

I=E2=80=99m going to spend some time reading up on Trial-observer MRDS an=
d may post a follow-up question at a later time.

Thanks for all of your help thus far,
Natalie.=20


Reply 1:

September 26, 2011

Any use of the photos to "correct" the visual observations would have to =
assume that: 1. all narwhal visible to observers are visible on the photo=
s; and 2. Photoanalysts do not miss narwhal that are visible on the photo=
s.=20

I don't think either of these assumptions is necessarily true for narwhal=
. For 1), observers might see animals ahead of the plane that were not vi=
sible on the photos, or the observers may detect the animal through movem=
ent but this would not be detectable on still photos. For 2), we all know=
observers miss animals, so why would we expect observers looking at phot=
os not to? This could however be estimated by taking a couple of blind pa=
sses through the photos, kind of like double platforms.

My limited experience with still photos leads me to believe that it is of=
ten very difficult to see animals on the photos, particularly if there ar=
e any waves at all. You can usually detect something if you know there is=
an animal in the photo (e.g. because it was detected by an observer at t=
he same time), but if you didn't know that, you would probably miss it.=20=


The photos should be useful for confirming group size and correcting dist=
ances, however.

You say that you have observers on each side who miss animals and who do =
not see animals that are not seen by the "good" observers. I guess we mig=
ht expect MRDS to estimate perfect detectability for the "good" observers=
and poor detectability for the "bad" ones. Are the good observers always=
on the same platform, or are they mixed? Are the platforms identical? If=
so, you could put the good observers on a separate platform, despite the=
actual seating position. If the observers are mixed, I guess you will en=
d up with g(0)<1 for both platforms. I am not sure which is the better wa=
y, I guess the overall combined g(0) will be the same.

Just some random thoughts, good luck.

Daniel Pike.


Reply 2:

September 27, 2011

You can use the photographic detections of animals to estimate the probab=
ility than a human observer detects an available animal in the overlap ar=
ea between human and camera search areas. To do this you do not need all =
photos or all photographed animals or all transect lines (unless transect=
line was an explanatory variable for human detection probability, but I'=
m sure it is not). All you need is locations of a decent number of animal=
s detected photographically and whether or not these were detected by an =
observer. If you searched only photos in areas of high animal density and=
used those as your trials in a Trial-observer MRDS configuration you'd g=
et an unbiased estimate of the human observers' detection functions - pro=
viding that there is nothing about the areas of high animal density that =
affects human observer detection probability. (If high density areas were=
low Beaufort areas, for example, you'd be getting a positively biased es=
timate of observer detection probability overall.)

David

Reply 3:
October 1, 2011

Sounds like a good case for reviewing observer data while the survey is g=
oing on, to try to correct problems before it's too late! Anyway, it's n=
ot a problem in theory to have different detection functions for differen=
t observers - you just need to estimate it. But an alternative is to poo=
l the observations for the two observers on each side of the plane (so lo=
ng as duplicates are clear) so you're fitting a platform rather then obse=
rver specific model.

For the photo data, in theory there is no problem with focussing on trans=
ects where animals were seen to screen your photos. Each narwhal you fin=
d on a photo represents a "trial" for the visual observers, and it doesn'=
t matter how you generate trials. The assumption is that trial outcomes =
are independent in the double observer model, given the covariates. Howe=
ver, in practice this is a bit dangerous because the double observer meth=
ods assume you get the detection function model right, and it might be th=
at something is affecting trackline detection probability in the low dens=
ity/low detectability transects that is not affecting it in the high dens=
ity/high detectability transects. So, taking observations from just the =
high count transects seems dangerous.=20

- len
